scenario.name: AuKill EDR Killer Abusing Signed Sysinternals PROCEXP152.SYS (BYOVD)
scenario.overview: Imagine a bustling coastal shipping port with blue harbor water, stacked colorful steel cargo containers, a towering yellow overhead gantry crane, and a moored cargo ship. Out on the concrete harbor pier, a worker notices a single shipping container whose side inspection hatch was accidentally left unlatched during loading. In this real-world scenario, the intruder approaches the harbor crane inspection pier disguised as a regular visitor, then bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the stacked cargo containers & ship. The port authority watchtower spots footsteps leaving a supposedly sealed container bay and compares the manifest seal numbers against the pier camera. In this scenario (T1543.003, AuKill EDR Killer Abusing Signed Sysinternals PROCEXP152.SYS (BYOVD)), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: dropping, then opening \\.\PROCEXP152, then ring-0 Termination of PPL EDR Sensors. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Dropping, then Opening \\.\PROCEXP152, then Ring-0 Termination of PPL EDR Sensors, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 6 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: Dropping & Registering Vulnerable Signed PROCEXP152.SYS v16.32
stages.subtitle: Privilege Escalation (T1543.003 - Windows Service / BYOVD)
stages.description: Out on the concrete harbor pier, a worker notices a single shipping container whose side inspection hatch was accidentally left unlatched during loading. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder approaches the harbor crane inspection pier disguised as a regular visitor while everyday visitors and the harbor customs inspector go about their routine. Running with local administrator rights, AuKill unpacked an embedded resource containing version 16.32 of PROCEXP152.SYS into C:\Windows\System32\drivers\PROCEXP152.SYS and loaded it via CreateServiceW / StartServiceW (bypassing Windows Driver Signature Enforcement because PROCEXP152.SYS v16.32 carries a valid Microsoft Windows Hardware Compatibility Publisher Authenticode signature). While newer versions of Sysinternals Process Explorer (v17.0+) added security descriptor checks restricting driver access, version 16.32 permitted any local administrator process to open its device object. In the documented EventID 6 exchange from AuKill User-Mode Controller to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK 6 (confirming that the Stage 1: Dropping & Registering Vulnerable Signed PROCEXP152.SYS v16.32 request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Opening \.PROCEXP152 & Issuing IOCTL 0x8335003C / 0x83350004). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Dropping & Registering Vulnerable Signed PROCEXP152.SYS v16.32 / ⇠#1 ACK 6) from Node ① (#1 AuKill User-Mode Controller) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Terminated PPL EDR & AV Services).

stages.title: Stage 2: Opening \\.\PROCEXP152 & Issuing IOCTL 0x8335003C / 0x83350004
stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion (T1562.001 - Disable or Modify Tools)
stages.description: Slipping out through that open container hatch while the yellow gantry crane swings overhead, the stowaway steps straight onto the restricted customs dockyard. Here in Step 2 inside the shipping port, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the harbor crane inspection pier in tiny disguised batches without disturbing the sealed bonded export yard. AuKill opened a file handle to \\.\PROCEXP152 and spawned multiple worker threads that enumerated running processes and handles, invoking DeviceIoControl with IOCTL 0x8335003C (IOCTL_OPEN_PROTECTED_PROCESS_HANDLE, which calls ZwOpenProcess from Ring-0 kernel mode to return a full-access handle to any Protected Process Light PID) and IOCTL 0x83350004 (IOCTL_CLOSE_HANDLE, which forces the kernel to close every active handle held by the target security service). Normally, Windows blocks user-mode administrators from opening PROCESS_TERMINATE handles to PsProtectedSignerAntimalware-Light (PPL) processes, but a ZwOpenProcess call originating from a Ring-0 kernel driver (KernelMode previous mode) bypasses PPL checks completely. Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ aukill.exe / ⇠#2 ALERT 1) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 SCM Service (PROCEXP152.SYS v16.32)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Terminated PPL EDR & AV Services).

stages.title: Stage 3: Ring-0 Termination of PPL EDR Sensors & Ransomware Detonation
stages.subtitle: Impact (T1486 - Data Encrypted for Impact)
stages.description: Now roaming freely outside the sealed steel box, the intruder walks across the shipping port pier and alters manifests bound for the moored cargo ship. In this final step inside the shipping port, the intruder bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the stacked cargo containers & ship until the port authority manifest watch catches the mismatch. Using the Ring-0 handle returned by 0x8335003C and the handle-closing primitive 0x83350004, AuKill continuously terminated processes and services matching Microsoft Defender (MsMpEng.exe), Sophos, Elastic, SentinelOne, and Carbon Black, clearing the way for immediate detonation of Medusa Locker or LockBit ransomware (AuKill keeps its worker threads running in the background during encryption so if the Windows Service Control Manager attempts to restart a crashed EDR service, AuKill kills the new PID within milliseconds In the documented EventID 5 exchange from SCM Service PROCEXP152SYS v1632 to DeviceIoControl 0x8335003C / 0004, DeviceIoControl 0x8335003C / 0004 responds with ACK 5 confirming that the Stage 3: Ring-0 Termination of PPL EDR Sensors & Ransomware Detonation request succeeded on DeviceIoControl 0x8335003C / 0004 and completing the final execution objective of AuKill EDR Killer Abusing Signed Sysinternals PROCEXP152SYS BYOVD). AuKill keeps its worker threads running in the background during encryption so if the Windows Service Control Manager attempts to restart a crashed EDR service, AuKill kills the new PID within milliseconds. In the documented EventID 5 exchange from SCM Service (PROCEXP152.SYS v16.32) to DeviceIoControl (0x8335003C / 0004), DeviceIoControl (0x8335003C / 0004) responds with ACK 5 (confirming that the Stage 3: Ring-0 Termination of PPL EDR Sensors & Ransomware Detonation request succeeded on DeviceIoControl (0x8335003C / 0004) and completing the final execution objective of AuKill EDR Killer Abusing Signed Sysinternals PROCEXP152.SYS (BYOVD)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: Ring-0 Termination of PPL EDR Sensors & Ransomware Detonation / ⇠#3 ACK 5) from Node ③ (#3 SCM Service (PROCEXP152.SYS v16.32)) to Node ④ (#4 DeviceIoControl (0x8335003C / 0004)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Terminated PPL EDR & AV Services).
